summary: Kyo Kano worked in Indology and philosophy. Kano studied at Keio University, Kyoto University, and the University of Vienna, and later held positions at Kyoto University (attested 1989) and Kobe Women's University (attested 2000).

Kyojun Shimizutani was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Keijun Shimizutani, at Tendai Sect University, and Taisho University. He served as professor at Tendai Sect University and Taisho University, and later became head priest of Senso-ji.
Kyoko Amano is a scholar of Indology and linguistics. She studied at Osaka University and the University of Freiburg, later holding academic posts at Osaka University and Kyoto University.

Kyoko Fujii is a Buddhist studies and Indology scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo. She held professorships at Hokkaido University and the International College for Postgraduate Buddhist Studies, and became Director of the International Institute for Buddhist Studies.
Kyoko Tokuno is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Sinology. She held positions at the University of Oregon and the University of Washington, where she was attested as professor in 2017.
Kyokuga Saeki was a Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar who studied under numerous traditional teachers, including Gen'yū and Reiga. He served as head abbot of Sennyu-ji from around 1876 to 1891.
Kyosho Hayashima was an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar. He held academic positions at Yokohama City University, Toyo University, and the University of Tokyo.
Kyosho Tanaka is a Buddhist studies scholar. He studied at the University of Tokyo from around 1966 to 1976 and served as an associate professor at Musashino University from around 1976 to 2017.
Kyoshun Todo was a Buddhist studies scholar who held posts as associate professor and professor at Bukkyo University.

Kyozo Yamada studied at the University of Tokyo and trained under traditional Zen masters including Sogaku Harada. Active in Buddhist studies and religious studies, he founded Kamakura Haku-un-kai and served as head of Sanbo Zen.

Kyōtarō Nishikawa was a scholar of archaeology, history, Japanology, and Buddhist studies who studied at Keio University. He served as Director-General of the Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties and worked at Kanagawa Prefectural Museum of Cultural History.

Károly Fiók was an Indologist who studied at Eötvös Loránd University, Humboldt University of Berlin, and the University of Munich. He worked as a teacher at Budapest Reformed High School and Debrecen Reformed College.
Käthe Marschner was an Indologist who completed her PhD at the University of Breslau in 1933 under Otto Strauss.

Käthe Neumann was a scholar of religious studies, Indology, and Buddhist studies. She earned her Ph.D. under Johannes Nobel at the University of Marburg and served as curator in charge of the Religionskundliche Sammlung from 1937 to 1968.
Kārlis Augusts Tennisons was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at Saint Petersburg State University and served as director of Datsan Gunzechoinei from 1906 to 1923.
Kōgi Kudara was a scholar of Buddhist studies, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He served as a professor at Ryukoku University from around 1979 to 2004.
Kōichi Kozaka is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Tibetology who studied under Hakuyu Hadano. He served as a professor at Osaka Kyoiku University.

Kōsen Imakita was a Zen master and scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy who trained under teachers including Gisan Zenkai. He served as abbot of Eikō-ji and Engaku-ji and worked as a Doctrinal Instructor for the Ministry of Religion.
Kōshō Ōtani was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at the First Higher School and Tokyo Imperial University, later succeeding Kozui Otani.
L. Johannes Frohnmeyer was an Indologist and linguist who studied at the Basel Mission. He served as an inspector of missions for the Basel Mission and was a Fellow of the University of Madras.
